topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Statistics
topic.scope: collection and presentation of data, histograms, frequency polygons, mean, median and mode of grouped data

nodes.name: Types of data and frequency tables
Class width = upper limit minus lower limit
Class mark = average of the two limits
Bars touch with no gaps for continuous classes
Bar height shows frequency when widths equal
Close polygon with zero-frequency classes at ends
Mean of ungrouped data = sum divided by count
Mean of grouped data uses class mark times frequency
Divide sum of f times x by sum of f
Data must be ordered before finding median
Median of even count is average of two middle values
Median class is where cumulative frequency reaches n/2
Mode is the most frequent value
Modal class has the highest frequency

misconceptions.statement: The frequency of a value is the value itself, so the frequency of 8 marks is 8.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the data value with the number of times it occurs.
misconceptions.fix: Frequency is how many times an observation occurs, not the observation's size.

probe.question: In marks 5, 8, 8, 9, 8, what is the frequency of 8?

misconceptions.root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student errors in reading frequency tables

misconceptions.statement: Data from a government report is primary data for any student who uses it.
misconceptions.why: Students think primary means important or official.
misconceptions.fix: Primary data is collected first-hand by the investigator; data taken from existing sources is secondary.

probe.question: A student copies population figures from a census book. Is this primary or secondary data?
probe.wrong_answer: Primary, because the source is official

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Class width of 10-20 is found by counting the numbers 10 to 20, so it is 11.
misconceptions.why: Counting both end numbers as in a list of whole numbers.
misconceptions.fix: Class width is upper limit minus lower limit, so 20 − 10 = 10.

probe.question: What is the class width of the class 20-30?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: In classes 10-20 and 20-30, the value 20 belongs to both classes.
misconceptions.why: Students see 20 written in both classes and assume it is counted in both.
misconceptions.fix: In exclusive classes the upper limit is not included; 20 belongs only to 20-30.

probe.question: Which class does the observation 20 fall in: 10-20 or 20-30?

misconceptions.root_belief: what is written twice is counted twice
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student difficulties with grouped frequency tables

misconceptions.statement: Classes like 10-19 and 20-29 can be used for continuous data with no change, since there is no gap problem.
misconceptions.why: Students treat all data as whole numbers and ignore values between 19 and 20.
misconceptions.fix: For continuous data, inclusive classes must be converted to true limits (9.5-19.5, 19.5-29.5) so no gap is left.

probe.question: Where does 19.4 go in classes 10-19 and 20-29?

misconceptions.root_belief: numbers are only whole numbers

misconceptions.statement: The class mark of 10-20 is the lower limit, 10.
misconceptions.why: Students think a class is named by its first number.
misconceptions.fix: The class mark is the midpoint: (10 + 20) ÷ 2 = 15.

probe.question: What is the class mark of 30-40?

misconceptions.root_belief: a label stands for the whole group

misconceptions.statement: Cumulative frequency is just the frequency of the class written again.
misconceptions.why: Students do not see the running total idea and copy the column.
misconceptions.fix: Cumulative frequency of a class is the sum of its frequency and all earlier frequencies.

probe.question: Frequencies are 4, 6, 5. What is the cumulative frequency of the third class?

misconceptions.root_belief: a new term means the old term

misconceptions.statement: A histogram is the same as a bar graph, so bars should have gaps between them.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over the bar-graph prototype learned in earlier classes.
misconceptions.fix: A histogram for continuous classes has bars joined with no gaps, because the classes continue one after another.

probe.question: Should bars in a histogram of marks 0-10, 10-20, 20-30 have gaps?

misconceptions.root_belief: a new thing is like a familiar one
misconceptions.source_hint: research on confusion between histograms and bar charts

misconceptions.statement: In a histogram with unequal class widths, the tallest bar is always the class with highest frequency.
misconceptions.why: Students have only seen equal widths, where height alone shows frequency.
misconceptions.fix: With unequal widths, height must be frequency per unit width (adjusted frequency) so area matches frequency.

probe.question: Class 0-10 has frequency 10 and class 10-30 has frequency 16. Which has the taller bar if heights are adjusted?

misconceptions.root_belief: height alone shows size
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on histogram interpretation with unequal intervals

misconceptions.statement: A histogram's horizontal axis shows frequency and the vertical axis shows the classes.
misconceptions.why: Students mix axes or reverse them as in a horizontal bar graph.
misconceptions.fix: The classes (variable) go on the x-axis and frequency goes on the y-axis.

probe.question: What do you put on the x-axis of a histogram of heights?

misconceptions.root_belief: order of axes does not matter

misconceptions.statement: A frequency polygon is drawn by joining the tops of the bar corners at the class limits.
misconceptions.why: Students join the visible corners of the histogram rather than midpoints.
misconceptions.fix: A frequency polygon joins points plotted at class marks (midpoints) with their frequencies.

probe.question: At which x-value is the point for class 20-30 plotted?

misconceptions.root_belief: use what is visible, not the defined rule

misconceptions.statement: A frequency polygon should end at the first and last plotted points, not touch the axis.
misconceptions.why: Students think only classes with data matter, so nothing extra is added.
misconceptions.fix: The polygon is closed by adding classes of zero frequency at both ends, so it touches the x-axis.

probe.question: Should a polygon for classes 10-20, 20-30 be extended to the x-axis?
probe.wrong_answer: No, stop at the last point

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: To find the mean, add the values and divide by the number of distinct values.
misconceptions.why: Repeated values are viewed as redundant, so they are counted once.
misconceptions.fix: Mean is the sum of all observations divided by the total number of observations, including repeats.

probe.question: Find the mean of 2, 2, 2, 8.

misconceptions.root_belief: repeats do not add information
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' conceptions of the arithmetic mean

misconceptions.statement: The mean of grouped data is the sum of class marks divided by the number of classes.
misconceptions.why: Students treat class marks as ordinary data and ignore the frequencies.
misconceptions.fix: Each class mark must be weighted by its frequency: mean = Σfx ÷ Σf.

probe.question: Class marks 5, 15 with frequencies 9, 1. What is the mean?

misconceptions.root_belief: all values count equally regardless of weight
misconceptions.source_hint: research on weighted mean and average misconceptions

misconceptions.statement: In the grouped mean formula, divide Σfx by the number of classes.
misconceptions.why: Students mix the number of rows with the number of observations.
misconceptions.fix: Divide Σfx by Σf, the total frequency, which is the total number of observations.

probe.question: Σfx = 400, Σf = 20, with 5 classes. What is the mean?

misconceptions.root_belief: counting rows is counting items

misconceptions.statement: The mean must be one of the values in the data set.
misconceptions.why: Students think the average is an actual typical member.
misconceptions.fix: The mean is a calculated balance point and may not equal any observation, or even be a whole number.

probe.question: Is 3.5 a possible mean of the data 2, 3, 4, 5?
probe.wrong_answer: No, 3.5 is not in the data

misconceptions.root_belief: a result must look like its inputs
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's understanding of average

misconceptions.statement: The median is the middle number in the list as given, without arranging it.
misconceptions.why: Students take the position in the written order as the middle.
misconceptions.fix: Data must first be arranged in ascending or descending order before the middle value is picked.

probe.question: Find the median of 9, 2, 7, 1, 5.

misconceptions.root_belief: order of presentation does not matter

misconceptions.statement: For an even number of observations, the median is the larger of the two middle values.
misconceptions.why: Students think the median must be an actual data point.
misconceptions.fix: With an even count, the median is the mean of the two middle observations.

probe.question: Find the median of 2, 4, 6, 10.

misconceptions.root_belief: a result must look like its inputs

misconceptions.statement: The median class is the class in the middle of the table by position.
misconceptions.why: Students use the odd/even middle idea without cumulative frequency.
misconceptions.fix: The median class is the first class whose cumulative frequency is at least n/2.

probe.question: A table has 5 classes with frequencies 2, 3, 20, 3, 2. Which is the median class?
probe.wrong_answer: The third class only because it is in the middle (by position, ignoring cumulative frequency)

misconceptions.root_belief: the middle position means the middle value

misconceptions.statement: For grouped data, n/2 is the median.
misconceptions.why: Students stop after the half-total step and report the number they found.
misconceptions.fix: n/2 is only the position used to find the median class; the median is then found with the formula.

probe.question: For total frequency 40, what is the median?

misconceptions.root_belief: a position is the same as a value

misconceptions.statement: The mode is the highest frequency, not the value that has it.
misconceptions.why: Students report the count of the largest group rather than the value.
misconceptions.fix: Mode is the observation that occurs most often; the frequency only tells how often.

probe.question: Data 3, 5, 5, 5, 7. What is the mode?

misconceptions.root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: research on confusion between mode and its frequency

misconceptions.statement: Every data set has exactly one mode.
misconceptions.why: Textbook examples usually have a single clear peak.
misconceptions.fix: A data set can have no mode, one mode, or more than one mode.

probe.question: How many modes does 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 have?

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: The modal class is the class with the largest class mark.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the biggest numbers with the most frequent.
misconceptions.fix: The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, whatever its limits.

probe.question: Classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30 have frequencies 8, 12, 5. Which is the modal class?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Mean, median and mode are always equal, so any one can replace another.
misconceptions.why: Students think they are three names for the same average.
misconceptions.fix: They are different measures and are equal only for symmetrical data; for moderately skewed data Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean.

probe.question: Mean is 20 and median is 18. What is the mode using the relation?

misconceptions.root_belief: different names mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student confusion among measures of central tendency

misconceptions.statement: The relation Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean can be written as Mode = 2 Median − 3 Mean.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the coefficients when memorising the formula.
misconceptions.fix: The relation is Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean; the 3 goes with the median and the 2 with the mean.

probe.question: Median 18, mean 20: find the mode.

misconceptions.root_belief: memorised rules can be reordered freely
